Set directory:
This sets the working directory, which is the folder where R will look for files to read and where it will save outputs.

```{r}
setwd("")
```


This reads a CSV file (sample1NFHSaugmentedAnon.csv) into a dataframe (india.df).
```{r}
india.df <- read.csv("sample1NFHSaugmentedAnon.csv")
```


This calculates the total number of missing values in each column of the dataframe (india.df) and prints the result.
```{r}
missing_values <- colSums(is.na(india.df))
print(missing_values)
```

colnames(india.df) lists the names of the columns in the dataframe.
str(india.df) shows the structure of the dataframe, including data types and the first few values in each column.
summary(india.df) provides summary statistics for each column in the df.

```{r}
colnames(india.df)

str(india.df)

summary(india.df)
```

This block calculates the mean, maximum, median, and standard deviation of the bmi_numeric column and then prints these statistics along with the summary of the column.
```{r}
# Calculate summary statistics for bmi_numeric
mean_bmi <- mean(india.df$bmi_numeric)
max_bmi <- max(india.df$bmi_numeric)
median_bmi <- median(india.df$bmi_numeric)
sd_bmi <- sd(india.df$bmi_numeric)

# Print the results
mean_bmi
max_bmi
median_bmi
sd_bmi

summary(india.df$bmi_numeric)
```

The first boxplot visualizes the distribution of bmi_numeric across the entire population.
The second boxplot shows the distribution of bmi_numeric grouped by the social group category, which has been converted to a factor variable (socialgroup).
```{r}
#BOXPLOTS
boxplot(india.df$bmi_numeric , xlab="BMI Numeric" , ylab="Population",
        main="BMI Numeric , All " , horizontal=TRUE)

india.df$socialgroup <- as.factor(india.df$socialgroup) #converted to factor

# Create a boxplot for bmi_numeric across socialgroup
boxplot(bmi_numeric ~ socialgroup, data = india.df,
        horizontal = TRUE,  
        main = "Boxplot of BMI Numeric by Social Group",
        xlab = "Social Group", 
        ylab = "BMI Numeric",
        col = "lightblue",
        border = "black")
```

This creates a histogram of the bmi_numeric variable with:

Custom color settings (green for the bars and black for the borders).
Set at intervals of 5 for better visualization of the BMI distribution.
```{r}
#HISTOGRAMS

# Set custom colors and point characters
my.col <- c("black", "green3")
my.pch <- c(1, 19)  # Open and solid circles

# Create a histogram for the bmi_numeric variable with custom breaks
hist(india.df$bmi_numeric,
     breaks=(0:ceiling(max(india.df$bmi_numeric, na.rm = TRUE)/5))*5,  # Custom breaks in steps of 5
     main="Distribution of BMI Numeric",
     xlab="BMI Numeric",
     ylab="Count of Individuals",
     col=my.col[2],  # Fill color green3
     border=my.col[1])  # Border color black
```

Generates a density plot of bmi_numeric, which is a smoothed version of a histogram, showing the distribution of BMI. The plot uses a blue line with increased thickness (lwd = 2).
```{r}
#DENSITY PLOTS
# Plot a density plot for the bmi_numeric variable
plot(density(india.df$bmi_numeric), 
     main = "Density Plot of BMI Numeric",
     xlab = "BMI Numeric",
     ylab = "Density",
     col = "blue",   # Color of the density line
     lwd = 2)        # Line width
```


Creates a beanplot to compare the distribution of bmi_numeric across different social groups.
```{r}
# Create a beanplot for bmi_numeric split by socialgroup
library(beanplot)

beanplot(bmi_numeric ~ socialgroup, data = india.df,
         horizontal = TRUE,       # Horizontal orientation
         yaxt = "n",              # Disable y-axis ticks
         what = c(0, 1, 1, 0),    # Hide the bean curve, show mean and data points
         log="",
         side = "second",         # Plot beans on the right side
         col = list("blue", "lightgreen","yellow","red"), # Custom color for the beans
         main = "BMI Numeric by Social Group", 
         xlab = "BMI Numeric",
         ylab = "Social Group")
# Customize the y-axis labels
axis(side = 2, at = 1:length(levels(india.df$socialgroup)), 
     labels = levels(india.df$socialgroup))
```

This scatterplot visualizes the relationship between age and bmi_numeric, setting custom axis limits. Horizontal and vertical dotted lines are added to indicate the mean values of bmi_numeric and age, respectively.
```{r}
#scatterplot

# Create a scatter plot for age and bmi_numeric
plot(india.df$age, india.df$bmi_numeric,
     col = "blue",  # Color for the points
     xlim = c(15, 55),  # Set limits for the x-axis (age)
     ylim = c(min(india.df$bmi_numeric, na.rm = TRUE), max(india.df$bmi_numeric, na.rm = TRUE)),  # Set y-axis limits based on bmi_numeric
     main = "Age vs. BMI Numeric",
     xlab = "Age (years)", 
     ylab = "BMI Numeric")

# Add a horizontal line for the mean of bmi_numeric
abline(h = mean(india.df$bmi_numeric, na.rm = TRUE), col = "dark blue", lty = "dotted")

# Add a vertical line for the mean of age
abline(v = mean(india.df$age, na.rm = TRUE), col = "dark blue", lty = "dotted")
```



This line reads another dataset (rintro-chapter4.csv) from an online source related to customer data.
```{r}
cust.df <- read.csv(paste("http://r-marketing.r-forge.r-project.org/",
                          "data/rintro-chapter4.csv", sep=""))
```

This provides a summary of the customer dataset (cust.df)
```{r}
summary(cust.df)
```

This section creates a  simple scatterplot that visualizes the relationship between customer age and credit.score
```{r}
plot(x=cust.df$age, y=cust.df$credit.score)
```

This plot refines the scatterplot by limiting the xlim and ylim ranges to specific values (age 15-55, credit score 500-900). It also adds horizontal and vertical dotted lines representing the mean credit score and mean age, respectively, and adds color 
```{r}
plot(cust.df$age, cust.df$credit.score, 
     col="blue",
     xlim=c(15, 55), ylim=c(500, 900), 
     main="Active Customers as of June 2014",
     xlab="Customer Age (years)", ylab="Customer Credit Score ")
abline(h=mean(cust.df$credit.score), col="dark blue", lty="dotted")
abline(v=mean(cust.df$age), col="dark blue", lty="dotted")
```


The scatterplot visualizes the relationship between store spend (store.spend) and online spend (online.spend) over the past 12 months for customers.
```{r}
# Scatterplot with skewed variables and color-coded factors
plot(cust.df$store.spend, cust.df$online.spend, 
     main="Customers as of June 2014", 
     xlab="Prior 12 months in-store sales ($)", 
     ylab="Prior 12 months online sales ($)", 
     cex=0.7)
```


The histogram breaks down customer store spend into intervals of $10, helping visualize the distribution of store sales.
```{r}
hist(cust.df$store.spend, 
     breaks=(0:ceiling(max(cust.df$store.spend)/10))*10,
     main="Customers as of June 2014", 
     xlab="Prior 12 months in-store sales ($)", 
     ylab="Count of customers")

```

This code first converts the email variable into a factor, indicating whether customers have an email on file.

Two scatterplots visualize the relationship between store and online spend, color-coded by whether the customer has an email on file. The second plot uses logarithmic scales on both axes.
```{r}

cust.df$email <- as.factor(cust.df$email)
                           
# Define custom colors and point characters
my.col <- c("black", "green3") 
my.pch <- c(1, 19) # R's symbols for solid and open circles (see ?points)

plot(cust.df$store.spend, cust.df$online.spend,
     cex=0.7,
     col=my.col[cust.df$email], pch=my.pch[cust.df$email], 
     main="Customers as of June 2014", 
     xlab="Prior 12 months in-store sales ($)", 
     ylab="Prior 12 months online sales ($)" )

# and then add a legend
legend(x="topright", legend=paste("email on file:", levels(cust.df$email)), 
       col=my.col, pch=my.pch)

plot(cust.df$store.spend + 1, cust.df$online.spend + 1,
     log="xy", cex=0.7,
     col=my.col[cust.df$email], pch=my.pch[cust.df$email],
     main="Customers as of June 2014", 
     xlab="Prior 12 months in-store sales ($)", 
     ylab="Prior 12 months online sales ($)" )
legend(x="topright", legend=paste("email on file:", levels(cust.df$email)), 
       col=my.col, pch=my.pch)



```

This sets up a 2x2 layout of plots showing the relationship between distance.to.store and spending in-store and online. Two plots use a logarithmic scale on both axes.

```{r}
par(mfrow=c(2, 2))
plot(cust.df$distance.to.store, cust.df$store.spend, main="store")
plot(cust.df$distance.to.store, cust.df$online.spend, main="online")
plot(cust.df$distance.to.store, cust.df$store.spend+1, log="xy", 
     main="store, log")
plot(cust.df$distance.to.store, cust.df$online.spend+1, log="xy", 
     main="online, log")
```


The pairs function creates a scatterplot matrix, which visualizes pairwise relationships between multiple variables
```{r}
# Scatterplot matrix
pairs(formula = ~ age + credit.score + email +
                  distance.to.store + online.visits + online.trans + 
                  online.spend + store.trans + store.spend,
      data=cust.df)

```


An enhanced version of the scatterplot matrix, using the scatterplotMatrix function from the car package, which provides more visual information.
```{r}
library(car)   # install if needed: install.packages("car")
```

```{r}
scatterplotMatrix(formula = ~ age + credit.score + email +
                    distance.to.store + online.visits + online.trans + 
                    online.spend + store.trans + store.spend, 
                  data=cust.df)

```
COVARIANCE


Both codes calculate the covariance between age and credit.score. The second part standardizes the covariance, giving the correlation coefficient between the two variables.
```{r}
cov(cust.df$age, cust.df$credit.score)

cov(cust.df$age, cust.df$credit.score)/
  (sd(cust.df$age)*sd(cust.df$credit.score))
```

CORRELATION

The first function calculates the correlation between age and credit.score. The second line performs a correlation test.
```{r}
cor(cust.df$age, cust.df$credit.score)


cor.test(cust.df$age, cust.df$credit.score)
```
This calculates a correlation matrix for selected columns of the dataset.
```{r}
# Correlation matrix
cor(cust.df[, c(2, 3, 5:12)])
```


The corrplot.mixed function creates a visually enhanced correlation plot where the upper part shows ellipses representing the strength and direction of correlations. The colorpanel is used to create a color gradient where red indicates negative correlations and blue indicates positive ones.
```{r}
library(corrplot)    # for correlation plot
library(gplots)      # for color interpolation
```

```{r}

corrplot.mixed(corr=cor(cust.df[ , c(2, 3, 5:12)], use="complete.obs"), 
               upper="ellipse", tl.pos="lt", 
               upper.col = colorpanel(50, "red", "gray60", "blue4"))
```
